title: Incident pipelines with Spooler
excerpt: How an incident investigation can be built using durable message queues.
content_html:
Hi there! As some of you might know, I recently launched spooler.sh – a simple, managed message queue.

In this article, I’d like to show you how simple it can be to build pipelines with clear consistency and durability properties.

The project we’re going to build is small, though very much in line with the trends of today: LLMs are involved.

We’ll build a distributed agentic AI swarm that would perform multi-step actions with limited or no human supervision to investigate…

In fact, we’ll build a simple program that spins up and shuts down workers depending on a queue backlog. The workers would pull incidents from a queue and ask an LLM to investigate them.

Meet the fluffy one

Building the tool I’m going to describe in this article took a couple of days, but then I realized it had taken a pretty nice shape and might be worth sharing with the world as a tool on its own, rather than just a showcase example.

So I called it Pagedog – a funny name rhyming with “watchdog” but for pages coming from a pager. It is written in Go, and so are the snippets below, though nothing in the design depends on the language.

A page, for those who have never been on call, is the alert that wakes up whoever is on call at the moment: something monitoring decided a human must see. The pager is whatever sends it, PagerDuty, incident.io and Alertmanager alike.

Design

On one side, we have a webhook handler for your observability stack – it receives pages from Prometheus Alertmanager, incident.io, PagerDuty, or whatever else you want to integrate with.

In many implementations I’ve seen, including systems I’ve built myself and approaches I’ve discussed with other engineers, the incoming page is usually stored somewhere before further processing. On the other hand, some of the implementations do not store it at all and simply process it straight away.

The risk of the latter approach is that you can lose the page, possibly along with wasted compute and LLM tokens. Depending on your observability stack and its retry behavior, the page might never arrive again, or arrive too late.

So what we’re going to do in this article is store the page in a message queue – specifically, a Spooler queue (what a nice coincidence!). This gives us useful guarantees around durability and delivery.

Once we’ve received the page and stored it in the queue as an incident, that’s already one half of our project. The second half is to pull it back from the queue and feed it to an LLM of our choice – we ask the LLM to analyze the incident and investigate what might have gone wrong.

Of course, we also need to give it access to some of our infrastructure observability tools. Otherwise, it won’t be able to do much beyond rephrasing the incident’s description. So we give the LLM access to our metrics, logs, and whatever else we want to provide.

 Alertmanager   |   webhook  ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐
 incident.io    |  --------> │ pagedog server │ ───▶ │ incident queue │
 ...            |            └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘
                |                                            │
                |                                            ▼
 MCPs           |            +----------------+      ┌────────────────┐
 Prometheus     |  <-------> |      LLMs      | <--> │ pagedog worker │
 ...            |            +----------------+      └────────────────┘
                |                                            │
                |                                            ▼
 Slack          |            ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐
 incident.io    |  ◀──────── │ pagedog server │ ◀─── │  report queue  │
 ...            |            └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘

The promised properties

Here is what this design gives us; the sections below deliver them one by one:

  • a page is never lost once the pager has heard 200 OK from us
  • a page sent twice comes down to one investigation
  • a worker that crashes mid-investigation is replaced, and its incident redelivered
  • a report, once written, is never lost on its way to the next stage
  • every destination hears of every report, at least once

Webhook

The webhook server is the plainest part here. It serves one route per source, e.g. /webhook/alertmanager, and the handler is anything that can turn an HTTP request into incidents:

type IncidentSource interface {
	Handle(*http.Request) ([]pagedog.Incident, error)
}

Each source first checks the page really comes from its pager: a bearer Authorization token, a signature over the body or anything else the source’s spec provides.

Then it reads the incidents out of the payload and passes them up the stack to be sent into the incidents queue: our system’s “edge” queue holding the input. Only when every send has succeeded does it answer 200 OK, confirming the input is in and is durable:

incs, err := src.Handle(req)
if errors.Is(err, ErrForbidden) {
	http.Error(res, "", http.StatusForbidden)
	return
}
if err != nil {
	http.Error(res, "failed parsing body", http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
}
for _, inc := range incs {
	if err := s.enqueue(req.Context(), inc); err != nil {
		// The source may retry the whole notification: the queue
		// deduplicates what was sent already.
		http.Error(res, "failed sending job", http.StatusBadGateway)
		return
	}
}
// 200 OK.

That ordering is the entire durability story of this part: the pager hears “got it” only once the incident is on the queue, and retries otherwise. The status codes are how we tell it: pagers retry on a 5xx and give up on a 4xx, so a bad token or a payload we can’t parse gets a 403 or a 400, which a retry wouldn’t fix, and a failed send gets a 502, so that the pager tries again.

This is where the first Spooler property shows up: deduplication. Every incident has a key the source derives from the page (in case of Alertmanager, the alert’s fingerprint and the time it started firing) and the queue is told to dedup by it:

incidents := spooler.Queue[pagedog.Incident]{
	Client: client,
	Spool:  "default",
	Queue:  "incidents",
	Dedup: func(inc pagedog.Incident) string {
		return inc.Key
	},
}

A second send with the same key within the queue’s dedup window – a setting of the queue, seconds to minutes long – is not a second message: a repeated page or a retried one comes down to one investigation. A page repeated after the window, as Alertmanager does for an alert still firing hours later, is a new message and a fresh investigation, and that’s intended: by then the picture may well have changed.

The Spool field above is, in SQL terms, a database: an isolation unit holding its queues, with its own write-ahead log, I/O and limits, so one spool never slows down another. Every account starts with one named default, and for Pagedog that one is enough.

Workers

Once the incident is on the queue, we need something that pumps it further down the pipeline: we need to spin up workers to do so.

In Pagedog, workers are, deliberately, a rather vague concept: the actual execution mechanism is hidden behind a runtime interface:

type Runtime interface {
	Stats(context.Context) (Stats, error)
	Launch(context.Context) (Worker, error)
	Shutdown(context.Context, Worker) error
}

A runtime implementation can range from goroutines running inside the process to separate containers or pods running on your platform, or functions for a serverless one. The interface allows us to keep these execution details separate from the rest of the system and plug in any compute.

How much to spin?

To understand when it needs to spin up another worker, Pagedog checks a few simple metrics from the Spooler queue: the number of currently visible messages in the incidents queue – that is, waiting to be received – and the number of messages already being processed by workers – that is, messages in pending state.

The sum gives us an estimate of how many workers we would ideally want to run to process all the available incidents. The number of running workers is bounded by configuration:

func desired(q QueueStats, minWorkers, maxWorkers int) int {
	want := int(q.Pending + q.Visible)
	want = min(want, maxWorkers)
	want = max(want, minWorkers)
	return want
}

The desired() is called from the runtime reconciler loop: periodically, it compares the number of running workers with the desired one, and launches or shuts down the difference.

Sniffing incidents out

The worker itself is very simple. It pulls messages from the incidents queue, where each message represents one incident that needs to be investigated.

For every incident, the worker talks to the configured LLM through its API:

type Model interface {
	Complete(context.Context, CompleteRequest) (CompleteResult, error)
}
type CompleteRequest struct {
	// Messages is the conversation so far: the task text, model replies
	// and tool output.
	Messages []Message

	// Tools holds the specs of the tools the model may call.
	Tools []ToolSpec
}

The LLM API is stateless, so every call carries the whole conversation. Along with it we send the specs of the tools: a name, a description and the schema of the input. The model answers either with text, or with a request to call one of the tools. In the latter case our code runs the tool, appends its output to the conversation and asks the model again. This repeats until the model answers with text alone – that is the report. Each round trip is a turn, and since every turn re-sends the conversation, turns are what the investigation costs.

As you can see, we pass the LLM the available tools’ specs, letting it use them in the interest of the investigation – for example, to fetch logs around the incident or read the source code involved in the logged activities.

Many systems today have MCP servers that can serve these needs. Pagedog has a generic MCP tool implementation that connects to those, as well as direct integrations with Prometheus and Loki as the built-in tools.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a protocol between a program driving a model and a server offering it tools. The server lists its tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema of its input, and runs a tool when asked, returning text. That listing is the same shape as the ToolSpec below, which is why Pagedog can hand an MCP server’s tools to the model without knowing what they do.

The built-in tools are read-only queries, while for MCP the model gets only the tools you list – the list is required, so nothing is granted by omission. The model’s reach into your infrastructure is exactly as far as you let it.

Adding a new tool requires implementing the Tool interface and wiring it up in the configuration:

// Tool is something the model may call.
type Tool interface {
	// Spec describes the tool to the model.
	Spec() ToolSpec

	// Call runs the tool on the model's input, which the model shaped after
	// Spec's schema. The text goes back to the model; so does an error.
	Call(ctx context.Context, input []byte) (string, error)
}

ToolSpec defines the structure of the input, so the model knows what the tool expects.

The initial message in the converstaion – the worker’s task for the model – is a text rendered from a template with the incident’s fields. The default one is short:

You are the on-call engineer. Investigate the incident below and write a short
report in Markdown: what happened, the evidence you found in the metrics and
the logs, the likely cause, and what to do next.

The incident started at {{.StartedAt}}; it is now {{.Now}}. Look at the window
from fifteen minutes before the start until now, and give the tools times in
RFC 3339.

The incident, as its source reported it:
---
{{.Raw}}
---

What comes back, once the model stops calling tools, is Markdown in the shape the task asks for: what happened, the evidence, the likely cause and what to do next.

Depending on how deep you want the investigation to go, all of this takes a while. And that is where the second Spooler property comes into play.

Leases and Retries

Spooler leases messages to consumers. This means that when a worker receives a message, it doesn’t immediately remove it from the queue: instead, the worker holds a lease of that message while processing it. The lease can expire, in which case the message is either re-delivered to another worker or enters the failed state if the retry budget is exhausted (the budget is the queue’s maxRetries setting).

The receive loop is as simple as:

for ctx.Err() == nil {
	m, ok, err := client.Recv(ctx, spooler.RecvRequest{
		Spool:       spool,
		Queue:       queue,
		WaitSeconds: new(1), // Wait up to one second for a message.
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if !ok {
		// No visible messages within the second: repeat.
		continue
	}
	process(ctx, m)
}

Since an LLM investigation can take some time, the worker periodically renews the message lease so it doesn’t lose it. If the worker crashes in the middle of an investigation, the lease will eventually expire, and another worker can pick up the same message and retry.

A failed renewal cancels the investigation’s context: the message is someone else’s now, and the ongoing investigation should be stopped:

for {
	select {
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return
	case <-time.After(time.Until(expiresAt) / 3 * 2):
		// Renew at two thirds of the lease, leaving a third as a
		// margin for a slow request.
	}
	res, err := client.Renew(ctx, spooler.RenewRequest{
		Spool: spool,
		Lease: lease.token,
	})
	if err != nil {
		cancel() // Cancel investigation context.
		break
	}
	expiresAt = res.LeaseExpiresAt
}

Once the investigation is finished, the worker settles the leased message in one of the ways:

  • acknowledges (acks) it on success, which removes it from the queue
  • negatively acknowledges it (nacks) to spend one retry and have it redelivered
  • releases it to return it to the queue without spending a retry (when the worker shuts down)
  • fails it to put it in the failed state until a human intervenes (encoding issues, version mismatch and so on)
  • discards it to delete it entirely

In code, the investigation returns the settlement it wants – the ack-and-send we’ll get to in a bit. In case of a failure, the settlement is decided by the error. res is the received message, and sub is a context that survives a shutdown just long enough to settle:

settle, err := investigate(ctx, item)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, ErrDiscard):
	settle = r.discard

case errors.Is(err, ErrFail):
	settle = r.fail

case err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil:
	// A shutdown or a lost lease is not the message's fault: a release
	// spends no retry.
	settle = r.release

case err != nil:
	settle = r.nack
}
_ = settle(sub, res.Lease)

Reports

Once the model finishes the investigation, we have a report. Now we need to decide what to do with it. Pagedog stores the report outside the message queue: a message queue isn’t really intended to serve as permanent storage for documents. Its contents are dynamic, and often queues have limits on how much data can be stored in a single message, Spooler included.

So we introduce another component into our stack, one the diagram above doesn’t show, sitting next to the worker – a report store:

// ReportStore persists incident reports that can be retrieved later.
type ReportStore interface {
	// Store keeps the report of the incident under its key and returns its
	// URI. The same incident stored again overrides anything stored before.
	Store(ctx context.Context, inc Incident, r Report) (*url.URL, error)

	// Load returns the report Store() kept at u.
	Load(ctx context.Context, u *url.URL) (Report, error)
}

Currently Pagedog has two report store backends: the local filesystem (if you wish to run it all on just one machine), and GitHub issues, where every report becomes an issue in a repository of yours, and the same incident reported again updates its issue.

As with all the interfaces before, extending this one with something like S3 or another distributed storage system should be straightforward.

Once the report is stored, we put a new message into another Spooler queue – reports, for notification processing. The message contains a reference to the stored report rather than the report itself.

And this brings us to one of my favorite parts of the design.

Atomic ack-and-send

This is the third, and a particularly useful Spooler property, the one I’d like to draw your attention to: it is what makes building pipelines easy.

Spooler provides an API called ack-and-send. It acknowledges a message in one queue and sends a new message to another queue in a single atomic operation.

In our case, we acknowledge the original incident message in the incidents queue and send a new message containing the report reference to the reports queue. If the operation fails, the incident message isn’t acknowledged, and the report message isn’t added. If it succeeds, both changes are committed.

Why atomic matters? Without it, we would have to pick an order of the incident ack and report send:

  • Ack first, then send: a crash in between loses the report, and the incident is gone with it
  • Send first, then ack: a crash in between leaves the incident leased, it gets redelivered, and we investigate it again, paying the model twice and sending a second report.

The usual way around is an outbox table or idempotency keys, i.e. more state of ours to keep. ack-and-send makes it the queue’s problem instead.

This is exactly the kind of consistency property I wanted Spooler to make easy to use. In Pagedog this is wrapped into a Pipe (an abstraction which someday I may add to the spooler/x subpackage for reuse): a thing that receives messages from one queue as an A, turns each into a B, and puts the B on another queue. The worker’s whole job is that function (trimmed here of the task templating):

pipe := &spooler.Pipe[pagedog.Incident, pagedog.Report]{
	Client: client,
	Spool:  "default",
	Input:  "incidents",
	Output: "reports",
}
err := pipe.Pump(ctx,
	func(ctx context.Context, inc pagedog.Incident) (r pagedog.Report, err error) {
		res, err := agent.Do(ctx, ai.DoRequest{
			Task:     task(inc), // Task text rendered.
			MaxTurns: maxTurns,  // Limit roundtrips with LLM.
		})
		if err != nil {
			return r, err
		}
		u, err := reportStore.Store(ctx, inc, pagedog.Report{
			Text: res.Output,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return r, err
		}
		return pagedog.Report{
			Incident:  inc,
			ReportURI: u,
		}, nil
	},
)

When the callback function succeeds, Pump settles the message using ack-and-send.

Reporting reports

Once the report has been stored and the new message has been placed in the reports queue, there’s just one remaining piece: notifying someone about the investigation results. Currently, this happens inside the main Pagedog process, in a separate goroutine which drains the reports queue in much the same way as the workers work the incidents one.

It leases a message, loads the corresponding report from the store, and tries to deliver it to all the destinations specified in your configuration. That might be a Slack channel, a note on a PagerDuty incident, an update to an incident.io incident, or whatever else you want to integrate with.

Once the report has been successfully delivered to all configured destinations, Pagedog acknowledges the message.

If any of the destinations refuses, the message is nacked and comes back later – to all the destinations again, including those which already got the report. That is, delivery here is at-least-once per destination: a Slack channel might see the same report twice, but none of the destinations will miss it. That’s the price of not keeping per-destination state anywhere.

This time, we don’t need the atomic ack-and-send – an incident goes through three states, queued, reported and notified, and this is the last of them, where a simple ack is enough to remove the message from the queue.

And that’s it.

Running Pagedog

All of this is now available as an open-source MIT-licensed project called Pagedog. The repository comes with a docker compose demo under examples/docker, with Prometheus, Alertmanager and Loki around a tiny HTTP server you can break on purpose, and a single-manifest Kubernetes deployment under examples/k8s.

Recently, the local in-memory Spooler image became free to use in your own infrastructure for your own purposes, development and production alike, which means you can use Pagedog without being a hosted Spooler service subscriber.

It keeps the queues in memory, so what a restart loses is what was in flight during those few minutes – and a still-firing alert comes back with the next Alertmanager repeat anyway. The reports live outside the queue, so nothing already written is lost.

Of course, there is still an option to get stronger persistence or greater scale if you need one – you can always sign up for a tier of the hosted Spooler service, which provides durable and replicated queues.

Conclusion

So that’s Pagedog.

It’s a relatively simple project, but I think it demonstrates quite nicely how you can build useful, reliable processing pipelines with Spooler without introducing too much complexity into your application.

In Pagedog we had only two stages for a message – incidents and reports, but you can easily add more in between, keeping the wiring simple and transitions atomic.

The queue takes care of message delivery, leases, retries, and the atomic transition between stages, leaving us to focus on the actual application logic.

I hope this gives you a useful idea of how Spooler can fit into your own infrastructure projects.

And if you find Pagedog useful, feel free to try it out, explore the code, or extend it with your own runtimes, investigation tools, and notification destinations – PRs are more than welcome!

Postscript

One last thing worth mentioning: there’s nothing particularly incident-specific about this design really.

I chose incident investigation because it’s a domain I’m familiar with and many people are as well. But the same architecture can be applied to pretty much any workflow, LLM-powered or not, especially when you want to run it in a distributed fashion rather than orchestrating everything from your laptop.

Imagine a GitHub issue describing some work to be done. A worker picks it up and starts an agent on the codebase; the pull request it opens lands on the next queue, where another worker reviews it and potentially schedules further work. Each stage runs on its own machines, with its own scaling and retries.

But the core remains the same – the runtime reconciler loop and the task queue semantics.

An LLM agent doesn’t have to be a process running on your laptop, and an agent workflow doesn’t have to live inside one long-running process. The main point here is that switching from one shape to the other doesn’t take much, once the buzzwords are trimmed off: with message queues and relatively simple workers, you can build distributed pipelines where individual steps take time, fail, retry, and hand work over to the next stage. Pagedog is just one example of what you can build with this pattern, and Spooler is one way to make the coordination between those stages reliable.

Thank you for reading!

In the latter case our code runs the tool, appends its output to the conversation and asks the model again. This repeats until the model answers with text alone – that is the report. Each round trip is a turn, and since every turn re-sends the conversation, turns are what the investigation costs.As you can see, we pass the LLM the available tools’ specs, letting it use them in the interest of the investigation – for example, to fetch logs around the incident or read the source code involved in the logged activities.Many systems today have MCP servers that can serve these needs. Pagedog has a generic MCP tool implementation that connects to those, as well as direct integrations with Prometheus and Loki as the built-in tools.MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a protocol between a program driving a model and a server offering it tools. The server lists its tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema of its input, and runs a tool when asked, returning text. That listing is the same shape as the ToolSpec below, which is why Pagedog can hand an MCP server’s tools to the model without knowing what they do.The built-in tools are read-only queries, while for MCP the model gets only the tools you list – the list is required, so nothing is granted by omission. The model’s reach into your infrastructure is exactly as far as you let it.Adding a new tool requires implementing the Tool interface and wiring it up in the configuration:// Tool is something the model may call. type Tool interface { // Spec describes the tool to the model. Spec() ToolSpec // Call runs the tool on the model's input, which the model shaped after // Spec's schema. The text goes back to the model; so does an error. Call(ctx context.Context, input []byte) (string, error) } ToolSpec defines the structure of the input, so the model knows what the tool expects.The initial message in the converstaion – the worker’s task for the model – is a text rendered from a template with the incident’s fields. The default one is short:You are the on-call engineer. Investigate the incident below and write a short report in Markdown: what happened, the evidence you found in the metrics and the logs, the likely cause, and what to do next. The incident started at {{.StartedAt}}; it is now {{.Now}}. Look at the window from fifteen minutes before the start until now, and give the tools times in RFC 3339. The incident, as its source reported it: --- {{.Raw}} --- What comes back, once the model stops calling tools, is Markdown in the shape the task asks for: what happened, the evidence, the likely cause and what to do next.Depending on how deep you want the investigation to go, all of this takes a while. And that is where the second Spooler property comes into play.Leases and RetriesSpooler leases messages to consumers. This means that when a worker receives a message, it doesn’t immediately remove it from the queue: instead, the worker holds a lease of that message while processing it. The lease can expire, in which case the message is either re-delivered to another worker or enters the failed state if the retry budget is exhausted (the budget is the queue’s maxRetries setting).The receive loop is as simple as:for ctx.Err() == nil { m, ok, err := client.Recv(ctx, spooler.RecvRequest{ Spool: spool, Queue: queue, WaitSeconds: new(1), // Wait up to one second for a message. }) if err != nil { return err } if !ok { // No visible messages within the second: repeat. continue } process(ctx, m) } Since an LLM investigation can take some time, the worker periodically renews the message lease so it doesn’t lose it. If the worker crashes in the middle of an investigation, the lease will eventually expire, and another worker can pick up the same message and retry.A failed renewal cancels the investigation’s context: the message is someone else’s now, and the ongoing investigation should be stopped:for { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return case <-time.After(time.Until(expiresAt) / 3 * 2): // Renew at two thirds of the lease, leaving a third as a // margin for a slow request. } res, err := client.Renew(ctx, spooler.RenewRequest{ Spool: spool, Lease: lease.token, }) if err != nil { cancel() // Cancel investigation context. break } expiresAt = res.LeaseExpiresAt } Once the investigation is finished, the worker settles the leased message in one of the ways:acknowledges (acks) it on success, which removes it from the queuenegatively acknowledges it (nacks) to spend one retry and have it redeliveredreleases it to return it to the queue without spending a retry (when the worker shuts down)fails it to put it in the failed state until a human intervenes (encoding issues, version mismatch and so on)discards it to delete it entirelyIn code, the investigation returns the settlement it wants – the ack-and-send we’ll get to in a bit. In case of a failure, the settlement is decided by the error. res is the received message, and sub is a context that survives a shutdown just long enough to settle:settle, err := investigate(ctx, item) switch { case errors.Is(err, ErrDiscard): settle = r.discard case errors.Is(err, ErrFail): settle = r.fail case err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil: // A shutdown or a lost lease is not the message's fault: a release // spends no retry. settle = r.release case err != nil: settle = r.nack } _ = settle(sub, res.Lease) ReportsOnce the model finishes the investigation, we have a report. Now we need to decide what to do with it. Pagedog stores the report outside the message queue: a message queue isn’t really intended to serve as permanent storage for documents. Its contents are dynamic, and often queues have limits on how much data can be stored in a single message, Spooler included.So we introduce another component into our stack, one the diagram above doesn’t show, sitting next to the worker – a report store:// ReportStore persists incident reports that can be retrieved later. type ReportStore interface { // Store keeps the report of the incident under its key and returns its // URI. The same incident stored again overrides anything stored before. Store(ctx context.Context, inc Incident, r Report) (*url.URL, error) // Load returns the report Store() kept at u. Load(ctx context.Context, u *url.URL) (Report, error) } Currently Pagedog has two report store backends: the local filesystem (if you wish to run it all on just one machine), and GitHub issues, where every report becomes an issue in a repository of yours, and the same incident reported again updates its issue.As with all the interfaces before, extending this one with something like S3 or another distributed storage system should be straightforward.Once the report is stored, we put a new message into another Spooler queue – reports, for notification processing. The message contains a reference to the stored report rather than the report itself.And this brings us to one of my favorite parts of the design.Atomic ack-and-sendThis is the third, and a particularly useful Spooler property, the one I’d like to draw your attention to: it is what makes building pipelines easy.Spooler provides an API called ack-and-send. It acknowledges a message in one queue and sends a new message to another queue in a single atomic operation.In our case, we acknowledge the original incident message in the incidents queue and send a new message containing the report reference to the reports queue. If the operation fails, the incident message isn’t acknowledged, and the report message isn’t added. If it succeeds, both changes are committed.Why atomic matters? Without it, we would have to pick an order of the incident ack and report send:Ack first, then send: a crash in between loses the report, and the incident is gone with itSend first, then ack: a crash in between leaves the incident leased, it gets redelivered, and we investigate it again, paying the model twice and sending a second report.The usual way around is an outbox table or idempotency keys, i.e. more state of ours to keep. ack-and-send makes it the queue’s problem instead.This is exactly the kind of consistency property I wanted Spooler to make easy to use. In Pagedog this is wrapped into a Pipe (an abstraction which someday I may add to the spooler/x subpackage for reuse): a thing that receives messages from one queue as an A, turns each into a B, and puts the B on another queue. The worker’s whole job is that function (trimmed here of the task templating):pipe := &spooler.Pipe[pagedog.Incident, pagedog.Report]{ Client: client, Spool: "default", Input: "incidents", Output: "reports", } err := pipe.Pump(ctx, func(ctx context.Context, inc pagedog.Incident) (r pagedog.Report, err error) { res, err := agent.Do(ctx, ai.DoRequest{ Task: task(inc), // Task text rendered. MaxTurns: maxTurns, // Limit roundtrips with LLM. }) if err != nil { return r, err } u, err := reportStore.Store(ctx, inc, pagedog.Report{ Text: res.Output, }) if err != nil { return r, err } return pagedog.Report{ Incident: inc, ReportURI: u, }, nil }, ) When the callback function succeeds, Pump settles the message using ack-and-send.Reporting reportsOnce the report has been stored and the new message has been placed in the reports queue, there’s just one remaining piece: notifying someone about the investigation results. Currently, this happens inside the main Pagedog process, in a separate goroutine which drains the reports queue in much the same way as the workers work the incidents one.It leases a message, loads the corresponding report from the store, and tries to deliver it to all the destinations specified in your configuration. That might be a Slack channel, a note on a PagerDuty incident, an update to an incident.io incident, or whatever else you want to integrate with.Once the report has been successfully delivered to all configured destinations, Pagedog acknowledges the message.If any of the destinations refuses, the message is nacked and comes back later – to all the destinations again, including those which already got the report. That is, delivery here is at-least-once per destination: a Slack channel might see the same report twice, but none of the destinations will miss it. That’s the price of not keeping per-destination state anywhere.This time, we don’t need the atomic ack-and-send – an incident goes through three states, queued, reported and notified, and this is the last of them, where a simple ack is enough to remove the message from the queue.And that’s it.Running PagedogAll of this is now available as an open-source MIT-licensed project called Pagedog. The repository comes with a docker compose demo under examples/docker, with Prometheus, Alertmanager and Loki around a tiny HTTP server you can break on purpose, and a single-manifest Kubernetes deployment under examples/k8s.Recently, the local in-memory Spooler image became free to use in your own infrastructure for your own purposes, development and production alike, which means you can use Pagedog without being a hosted Spooler service subscriber.It keeps the queues in memory, so what a restart loses is what was in flight during those few minutes – and a still-firing alert comes back with the next Alertmanager repeat anyway. The reports live outside the queue, so nothing already written is lost.Of course, there is still an option to get stronger persistence or greater scale if you need one – you can always sign up for a tier of the hosted Spooler service, which provides durable and replicated queues.ConclusionSo that’s Pagedog.It’s a relatively simple project, but I think it demonstrates quite nicely how you can build useful, reliable processing pipelines with Spooler without introducing too much complexity into your application.In Pagedog we had only two stages for a message – incidents and reports, but you can easily add more in between, keeping the wiring simple and transitions atomic.The queue takes care of message delivery, leases, retries, and the atomic transition between stages, leaving us to focus on the actual application logic.I hope this gives you a useful idea of how Spooler can fit into your own infrastructure projects.And if you find Pagedog useful, feel free to try it out, explore the code, or extend it with your own runtimes, investigation tools, and notification destinations – PRs are more than welcome!PostscriptOne last thing worth mentioning: there’s nothing particularly incident-specific about this design really.I chose incident investigation because it’s a domain I’m familiar with and many people are as well. But the same architecture can be applied to pretty much any workflow, LLM-powered or not, especially when you want to run it in a distributed fashion rather than orchestrating everything from your laptop.Imagine a GitHub issue describing some work to be done. A worker picks it up and starts an agent on the codebase; the pull request it opens lands on the next queue, where another worker reviews it and potentially schedules further work. Each stage runs on its own machines, with its own scaling and retries.But the core remains the same – the runtime reconciler loop and the task queue semantics.An LLM agent doesn’t have to be a process running on your laptop, and an agent workflow doesn’t have to live inside one long-running process. The main point here is that switching from one shape to the other doesn’t take much, once the buzzwords are trimmed off: with message queues and relatively simple workers, you can build distributed pipelines where individual steps take time, fail, retry, and hand work over to the next stage. Pagedog is just one example of what you can build with this pattern, and Spooler is one way to make the coordination between those stages reliable.Thank you for reading!Referencesspooler.shdocs.spooler.shpagedog.devmodelcontextprotocol.io

content_html_zh:
你好呀！ As some of you might know, I recently launched spooler.sh – a simple, managed message queue.

In this article, I’d like to show you how simple it can be to build pipelines with clear consistency and durability properties.

The project we’re going to build is small, though very much in line with the trends of today: LLMs are involved.

We’ll build a distributed agentic AI swarm that would perform multi-step actions with limited or no human supervision to investigate…

In fact, we’ll build a simple program that spins up and shuts down workers depending on a queue backlog. The workers would pull incidents from a queue and ask an LLM to investigate them.

Meet the fluffy one

Building the tool I’m going to describe in this article took a couple of days, but then I realized it had taken a pretty nice shape and might be worth sharing with the world as a tool on its own, rather than just a showcase example.

So I called it Pagedog – a funny name rhyming with “watchdog” but for pages coming from a pager. It is written in Go, and so are the snippets below, though nothing in the design depends on the language.

A page, for those who have never been on call, is the alert that wakes up whoever is on call at the moment: something monitoring decided a human must see. The pager is whatever sends it, PagerDuty, incident.io and Alertmanager alike.

设计

On one side, we have a webhook handler for your observability stack – it receives pages from Prometheus Alertmanager, incident.io, PagerDuty, or whatever else you want to integrate with.

In many implementations I’ve seen, including systems I’ve built myself and approaches I’ve discussed with other engineers, the incoming page is usually stored somewhere before further processing. On the other hand, some of the implementations do not store it at all and simply process it straight away.

The risk of the latter approach is that you can lose the page, possibly along with wasted compute and LLM tokens. Depending on your observability stack and its retry behavior, the page might never arrive again, or arrive too late.

So what we’re going to do in this article is store the page in a message queue – specifically, a Spooler queue (what a nice coincidence!). This gives us useful guarantees around durability and delivery.

Once we’ve received the page and stored it in the queue as an incident, that’s already one half of our project. The second half is to pull it back from the queue and feed it to an LLM of our choice – we ask the LLM to analyze the incident and investigate what might have gone wrong.

Of course, we also need to give it access to some of our infrastructure observability tools. Otherwise, it won’t be able to do much beyond rephrasing the incident’s description. So we give the LLM access to our metrics, logs, and whatever else we want to provide.

 Alertmanager   |   webhook  ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐
 incident.io    |  --------> │ pagedog server │ ───▶ │ incident queue │
 ...            |            └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘
                |                                            │
                |                                            ▼
 MCPs           |            +----------------+      ┌────────────────┐
 Prometheus     |  <-------> |      LLMs      | <--> │ pagedog worker │
 ...            |            +----------------+      └────────────────┘
                |                                            │
                |                                            ▼
 Slack          |            ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐
 incident.io    |  ◀──────── │ pagedog server │ ◀─── │  report queue  │
 ...            |            └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘

The promised properties

Here is what this design gives us; the sections below deliver them one by one:

  • a page is never lost once the pager has heard 200 OK from us
  • a page sent twice comes down to one investigation
  • a worker that crashes mid-investigation is replaced, and its incident redelivered
  • a report, once written, is never lost on its way to the next stage
  • every destination hears of every report, at least once

网络钩子

The webhook server is the plainest part here. It serves one route per source, e.g. /webhook/alertmanager, and the handler is anything that can turn an HTTP request into incidents:

type IncidentSource interface {
	Handle(*http.Request) ([]pagedog.Incident, error)
}

Each source first checks the page really comes from its pager: a bearer Authorization token, a signature over the body or anything else the source’s spec provides.

Then it reads the incidents out of the payload and passes them up the stack to be sent into the incidents queue: our system’s “edge” queue holding the input. Only when every send has succeeded does it answer 200 OK, confirming the input is in and is durable:

incs, err := src.Handle(req)
if errors.Is(err, ErrForbidden) {
	http.Error(res, "", http.StatusForbidden)
	return
}
if err != nil {
	http.Error(res, "failed parsing body", http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
}
for _, inc := range incs {
	if err := s.enqueue(req.Context(), inc); err != nil {
		// The source may retry the whole notification: the queue
		// deduplicates what was sent already.
		http.Error(res, "failed sending job", http.StatusBadGateway)
		return
	}
}
// 200 OK.

That ordering is the entire durability story of this part: the pager hears “got it” only once the incident is on the queue, and retries otherwise. The status codes are how we tell it: pagers retry on a 5xx and give up on a 4xx, so a bad token or a payload we can’t parse gets a 403 or a 400, which a retry wouldn’t fix, and a failed send gets a 502, so that the pager tries again.

This is where the first Spooler property shows up: deduplication. Every incident has a key the source derives from the page (in case of Alertmanager, the alert’s fingerprint and the time it started firing) and the queue is told to dedup by it:

incidents := spooler.Queue[pagedog.Incident]{
	Client: client,
	Spool:  "default",
	Queue:  "incidents",
	Dedup: func(inc pagedog.Incident) string {
		return inc.Key
	},
}

A second send with the same key within the queue’s dedup window – a setting of the queue, seconds to minutes long – is not a second message: a repeated page or a retried one comes down to one investigation. A page repeated after the window, as Alertmanager does for an alert still firing hours later, is a new message and a fresh investigation, and that’s intended: by then the picture may well have changed.

The Spool field above is, in SQL terms, a database: an isolation unit holding its queues, with its own write-ahead log, I/O and limits, so one spool never slows down another. Every account starts with one named default, and for Pagedog that one is enough.

Workers

Once the incident is on the queue, we need something that pumps it further down the pipeline: we need to spin up workers to do so.

In Pagedog, workers are, deliberately, a rather vague concept: the actual execution mechanism is hidden behind a runtime interface:

type Runtime interface {
	Stats(context.Context) (Stats, error)
	Launch(context.Context) (Worker, error)
	Shutdown(context.Context, Worker) error
}

A runtime implementation can range from goroutines running inside the process to separate containers or pods running on your platform, or functions for a serverless one. The interface allows us to keep these execution details separate from the rest of the system and plug in any compute.

How much to spin?

To understand when it needs to spin up another worker, Pagedog checks a few simple metrics from the Spooler queue: the number of currently visible messages in the incidents queue – that is, waiting to be received – and the number of messages already being processed by workers – that is, messages in pending state.

The sum gives us an estimate of how many workers we would ideally want to run to process all the available incidents. The number of running workers is bounded by configuration:

func desired(q QueueStats, minWorkers, maxWorkers int) int {
	want := int(q.Pending + q.Visible)
	want = min(want, maxWorkers)
	want = max(want, minWorkers)
	return want
}

The desired() is called from the runtime reconciler loop: periodically, it compares the number of running workers with the desired one, and launches or shuts down the difference.

Sniffing incidents out

The worker itself is very simple. It pulls messages from the incidents queue, where each message represents one incident that needs to be investigated.

For every incident, the worker talks to the configured LLM through its API:

type Model interface {
	Complete(context.Context, CompleteRequest) (CompleteResult, error)
}
type CompleteRequest struct {
	// Messages is the conversation so far: the task text, model replies
	// and tool output.
	Messages []Message

	// Tools holds the specs of the tools the model may call.
	Tools []ToolSpec
}
The LLM API is stateless, so every call carries the whole conversation. Along with it we send the specs of the tools: a name, a description and the schema of the input. The model answers either with text, or with a request to call one of the tools. In the latter case our code runs the tool, appends its output to the conversation and asks the model again. This repeats until the model answers with text alone – that is the report. Each round trip is a turn, and since every turn re-sends the conversation, turns are what the investigation costs.

As you can see, we pass the LLM the available tools’ specs, letting it use them in the interest of the investigation – for example, to fetch logs around the incident or read the source code involved in the logged activities.

Many systems today have MCP servers that can serve these needs. Pagedog has a generic MCP tool implementation that connects to those, as well as direct integrations with Prometheus and Loki as the built-in tools.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a protocol between a program driving a model and a server offering it tools. The server lists its tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema of its input, and runs a tool when asked, returning text. That listing is the same shape as the ToolSpec below, which is why Pagedog can hand an MCP server’s tools to the model without knowing what they do.

The built-in tools are read-only queries, while for MCP the model gets only the tools you list – the list is required, so nothing is granted by omission. The model’s reach into your infrastructure is exactly as far as you let it.

Adding a new tool requires implementing the Tool interface and wiring it up in the configuration:

// Tool is something the model may call.
type Tool interface {
	// Spec describes the tool to the model.
	Spec() ToolSpec

	// Call runs the tool on the model's input, which the model shaped after
	// Spec's schema. The text goes back to the model; so does an error.
	Call(ctx context.Context, input []byte) (string, error)
}

ToolSpec defines the structure of the input, so the model knows what the tool expects.

The initial message in the converstaion – the worker’s task for the model – is a text rendered from a template with the incident’s fields. The default one is short:

You are the on-call engineer. Investigate the incident below and write a short
report in Markdown: what happened, the evidence you found in the metrics and
the logs, the likely cause, and what to do next.

The incident started at {{.StartedAt}}; it is now {{.Now}}. Look at the window
from fifteen minutes before the start until now, and give the tools times in
RFC 3339.

The incident, as its source reported it:
---
{{.Raw}}
---

What comes back, once the model stops calling tools, is Markdown in the shape the task asks for: what happened, the evidence, the likely cause and what to do next.

Depending on how deep you want the investigation to go, all of this takes a while. And that is where the second Spooler property comes into play.

Leases and Retries

Spooler leases messages to consumers. This means that when a worker receives a message, it doesn’t immediately remove it from the queue: instead, the worker holds a lease of that message while processing it. The lease can expire, in which case the message is either re-delivered to another worker or enters the failed state if the retry budget is exhausted (the budget is the queue’s maxRetries setting).

The receive loop is as simple as:

for ctx.Err() == nil {
	m, ok, err := client.Recv(ctx, spooler.RecvRequest{
		Spool:       spool,
		Queue:       queue,
		WaitSeconds: new(1), // Wait up to one second for a message.
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if !ok {
		// No visible messages within the second: repeat.
		continue
	}
	process(ctx, m)
}

Since an LLM investigation can take some time, the worker periodically renews the message lease so it doesn’t lose it. If the worker crashes in the middle of an investigation, the lease will eventually expire, and another worker can pick up the same message and retry.

A failed renewal cancels the investigation’s context: the message is someone else’s now, and the ongoing investigation should be stopped:

for {
	select {
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return
	case <-time.After(time.Until(expiresAt) / 3 * 2):
		// Renew at two thirds of the lease, leaving a third as a
		// margin for a slow request.
	}
	res, err := client.Renew(ctx, spooler.RenewRequest{
		Spool: spool,
		Lease: lease.token,
	})
	if err != nil {
		cancel() // Cancel investigation context.
		break
	}
	expiresAt = res.LeaseExpiresAt
}

Once the investigation is finished, the worker settles the leased message in one of the ways:

  • acknowledges (acks) it on success, which removes it from the queue
  • negatively acknowledges it (nacks) to spend one retry and have it redelivered
  • releases it to return it to the queue without spending a retry (when the worker shuts down)
  • fails it to put it in the failed state until a human intervenes (encoding issues, version mismatch and so on)
  • discards it to delete it entirely

In code, the investigation returns the settlement it wants – the ack-and-send we’ll get to in a bit. In case of a failure, the settlement is decided by the error. res is the received message, and sub is a context that survives a shutdown just long enough to settle:

settle, err := investigate(ctx, item)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, ErrDiscard):
	settle = r.discard

case errors.Is(err, ErrFail):
	settle = r.fail

case err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil:
	// A shutdown or a lost lease is not the message's fault: a release
	// spends no retry.
	settle = r.release

case err != nil:
	settle = r.nack
}
_ = settle(sub, res.Lease)

Reports

Once the model finishes the investigation, we have a report. Now we need to decide what to do with it. Pagedog stores the report outside the message queue: a message queue isn’t really intended to serve as permanent storage for documents. Its contents are dynamic, and often queues have limits on how much data can be stored in a single message, Spooler included.

So we introduce another component into our stack, one the diagram above doesn’t show, sitting next to the worker – a report store:

// ReportStore persists incident reports that can be retrieved later.
type ReportStore interface {
	// Store keeps the report of the incident under its key and returns its
	// URI. The same incident stored again overrides anything stored before.
	Store(ctx context.Context, inc Incident, r Report) (*url.URL, error)

	// Load returns the report Store() kept at u.
	Load(ctx context.Context, u *url.URL) (Report, error)
}

Currently Pagedog has two report store backends: the local filesystem (if you wish to run it all on just one machine), and GitHub issues, where every report becomes an issue in a repository of yours, and the same incident reported again updates its issue.

As with all the interfaces before, extending this one with something like S3 or another distributed storage system should be straightforward.

Once the report is stored, we put a new message into another Spooler queue – reports, for notification processing. The message contains a reference to the stored report rather than the report itself.

And this brings us to one of my favorite parts of the design.

Atomic ack-and-send

This is the third, and a particularly useful Spooler property, the one I’d like to draw your attention to: it is what makes building pipelines easy.

Spooler provides an API called ack-and-send. It acknowledges a message in one queue and sends a new message to another queue in a single atomic operation.

In our case, we acknowledge the original incident message in the incidents queue and send a new message containing the report reference to the reports queue. If the operation fails, the incident message isn’t acknowledged, and the report message isn’t added. If it succeeds, both changes are committed.

Why atomic matters? Without it, we would have to pick an order of the incident ack and report send:Ack first, then send: a crash in between loses the report, and the incident is gone with itSend first, then ack: a crash in between leaves the incident leased, it gets redelivered, and we investigate it again, paying the model twice and sending a second report.The usual way around is an outbox table or idempotency keys, i.e. more state of ours to keep. ack-and-send makes it the queue’s problem instead.

This is exactly the kind of consistency property I wanted Spooler to make easy to use. In Pagedog this is wrapped into a Pipe (an abstraction which someday I may add to the spooler/x subpackage for reuse): a thing that receives messages from one queue as an A, turns each into a B, and puts the B on another queue. The worker’s whole job is that function (trimmed here of the task templating):

pipe := &spooler.Pipe[pagedog.Incident, pagedog.Report]{
	Client: client,
	Spool:  "default",
	Input:  "incidents",
	Output: "reports",
}
err := pipe.Pump(ctx,
	func(ctx context.Context, inc pagedog.Incident) (r pagedog.Report, err error) {
		res, err := agent.Do(ctx, ai.DoRequest{
			Task:     task(inc), // Task text rendered.
			MaxTurns: maxTurns,  // Limit roundtrips with LLM.
		})
		if err != nil {
			return r, err
		}
		u, err := reportStore.Store(ctx, inc, pagedog.Report{
			Text: res.Output,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return r, err
		}
		return pagedog.Report{
			Incident:  inc,
			ReportURI: u,
		}, nil
	},
)

When the callback function succeeds, Pump settles the message using ack-and-send.

Reporting reports

Once the report has been stored and the new message has been placed in the reports queue, there’s just one remaining piece: notifying someone about the investigation results. Currently, this happens inside the main Pagedog process, in a separate goroutine which drains the reports queue in much the same way as the workers work the incidents one.

It leases a message, loads the corresponding report from the store, and tries to deliver it to all the destinations specified in your configuration. That might be a Slack channel, a note on a PagerDuty incident, an update to an incident.io incident, or whatever else you want to integrate with.

Once the report has been successfully delivered to all configured destinations, Pagedog acknowledges the message.

If any of the destinations refuses, the message is nacked and comes back later – to all the destinations again, including those which already got the report. That is, delivery here is at-least-once per destination: a Slack channel might see the same report twice, but none of the destinations will miss it. That’s the price of not keeping per-destination state anywhere.

This time, we don’t need the atomic ack-and-send – an incident goes through three states, queued, reported and notified, and this is the last of them, where a simple ack is enough to remove the message from the queue.

And that’s it.

Running Pagedog

All of this is now available as an open-source MIT-licensed project called Pagedog. The repository comes with a docker compose demo under examples/docker, with Prometheus, Alertmanager and Loki around a tiny HTTP server you can break on purpose, and a single-manifest Kubernetes deployment under examples/k8s.

Recently, the local in-memory Spooler image became free to use in your own infrastructure for your own purposes, development and production alike, which means you can use Pagedog without being a hosted Spooler service subscriber.

It keeps the queues in memory, so what a restart loses is what was in flight during those few minutes – and a still-firing alert comes back with the next Alertmanager repeat anyway. The reports live outside the queue, so nothing already written is lost.

Of course, there is still an option to get stronger persistence or greater scale if you need one – you can always sign up for a tier of the hosted Spooler service, which provides durable and replicated queues.

结论

So that’s Pagedog.

It’s a relatively simple project, but I think it demonstrates quite nicely how you can build useful, reliable processing pipelines with Spooler without introducing too much complexity into your application.

In Pagedog we had only two stages for a message – incidents and reports, but you can easily add more in between, keeping the wiring simple and transitions atomic.

The queue takes care of message delivery, leases, retries, and the atomic transition between stages, leaving us to focus on the actual application logic.

I hope this gives you a useful idea of how Spooler can fit into your own infrastructure projects.

And if you find Pagedog useful, feel free to try it out, explore the code, or extend it with your own runtimes, investigation tools, and notification destinations – PRs are more than welcome!

后记

One last thing worth mentioning: there’s nothing particularly incident-specific about this design really.

I chose incident investigation because it’s a domain I’m familiar with and many people are as well. But the same architecture can be applied to pretty much any workflow, LLM-powered or not, especially when you want to run it in a distributed fashion rather than orchestrating everything from your laptop.

Imagine a GitHub issue describing some work to be done. A worker picks it up and starts an agent on the codebase; the pull request it opens lands on the next queue, where another worker reviews it and potentially schedules further work. Each stage runs on its own machines, with its own scaling and retries.

But the core remains the same – the runtime reconciler loop and the task queue semantics.

An LLM agent doesn’t have to be a process running on your laptop, and an agent workflow doesn’t have to live inside one long-running process. The main point here is that switching from one shape to the other doesn’t take much, once the buzzwords are trimmed off: with message queues and relatively simple workers, you can build distributed pipelines where individual steps take time, fail, retry, and hand work over to the next stage. Pagedog is just one example of what you can build with this pattern, and Spooler is one way to make the coordination between those stages reliable.
